subsection: 5. The decline of Cold War certainties, 1973–1989: withdrawal from Vietnam, détente, SALT and Star Wars

notes.h: The Cold War frame: containment, internationalism and technology
notes.b: By 1973 American foreign policy rested on ideas set in the late 1940s, and Vietnam had begun to shake them. Three ideas help the later blocks make sense: containment, internationalism and technological development.
points: Containment was the policy, in place since 1947, of stopping the spread of communism by resisting Soviet expansion. The arms race and mutual deterrence (each side stayed safe because the other feared nuclear retaliation) grew out of it.

Internationalism means a continuing US commitment to active engagement in world affairs. After Vietnam Americans debated how far that commitment should go, which is why this period matters for the whole story of US foreign policy.

Technological development means weapons and space systems that shaped the arms race, such as MIRVs (missiles carrying several warheads, each aimed at a different target), missile defence and verification satellites, which let each side check the other's arsenal.

Vietnam is the background to the period. Johnson's escalation, the Tet Offensive of 1968, the anti-war movement and Nixon's Vietnamisation (handing the fighting to South Vietnamese forces) had already weakened support for the war.
Nixon resigned over Watergate on 9 August 1974, so three presidents followed in this period: Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter (1977 to 1981) and Ronald Reagan (1981 to 1989).
notes.tip: For a Higher Level essay on US foreign policy from 1973 to 1989, build a clear line: retreat from Vietnam, détente at its height, collapse after 1979, Reagan's build-up, then negotiation with Gorbachev. Marks go to a judgement on continuity or change and to dated events in order.

notes.h: Leaving Vietnam: the Paris Peace Accords and Congress, 1973
notes.b: The United States left Vietnam in 1973 through a negotiated settlement, and Congress then closed off the option of fighting again. This weakened the consensus behind containment.
points: The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973 by the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government (the Viet Cong). They provided for a ceasefire, US withdrawal and the release of prisoners of war.

Kissinger and Le Duc Tho negotiated the Accords and were awarded the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize, though Le Duc Tho declined it. North Vietnamese troops were allowed to remain in the South, which left South Vietnam exposed once the Americans had gone.
The last US combat troops left by 29 March 1973, and American prisoners of war were released in the same weeks.

Congress passed the War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto on 7 November 1973 (House 284 to 135, Senate 75 to 18). It requires the President to consult and report to Congress and to withdraw forces within 60 days, with a 30-day extension for withdrawal, unless Congress authorises them.

The War Powers Resolution was meant to stop another undeclared war like Vietnam, because it put limits on a President sending troops abroad without Congress. Do not confuse it with the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of 1964, which had given Johnson wide powers.

The Case-Church amendment barred funds for US combat in Indochina from 15 August 1973. So when the North later broke the Accords, the United States could not intervene, and South Vietnam relied on its own forces and on aid from Congress.
notes.tip: Keep the two dates apart: the US left in 1973, but South Vietnam did not fall until 1975. Examiners ask why the US left in 1973 and why Saigon fell in 1975, and the War Powers Resolution is not the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.

notes.h: The fall of Saigon and the legacy of Vietnam, 1975
notes.b: Two years after American troops left, South Vietnam collapsed. The defeat left Americans cautious about overseas commitments and changed the debate about internationalism.
points: The North Vietnamese offensive of 1975 overran South Vietnam. In April 1975 Congress refused President Ford's request for emergency aid for South Vietnam, which showed how far the American consensus behind the war had collapsed.
Ford, not Nixon, was president when Saigon fell. Speaking at Tulane University, New Orleans, on 23 April 1975, he said that the war was finished as far as America was concerned.
Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. Operation Frequent Wind evacuated Americans and many South Vietnamese by helicopter on 29 and 30 April, so images of the evacuation became the symbol of the defeat.

Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, fell to the Khmer Rouge on 17 April 1975, and the communist Pathet Lao took power in Laos in December 1975. All three Indochinese states therefore had communist governments by the end of 1975.
About 58,000 Americans died in the war. The defeat produced the Vietnam syndrome, a reluctance to commit US forces abroad, which made later presidents cautious about overseas military commitments.
notes.tip: Remember that Ford was president at Saigon's fall. Give Ford's Tulane speech as reported speech, not as a quotation.

notes.h: Détente: Nixon, Kissinger and the opening to China and Moscow, 1969 to 1972
notes.b: Détente means the easing of tensions through negotiation, based on a balance of power rather than on trust. Nixon and Kissinger used it to manage rivalry with both communist giants while the US was weakened by Vietnam.
points: Henry Kissinger was national security adviser from 1969 and Secretary of State as well from 1973. He aimed for a stable balance of power in which no side could easily gain an advantage.
His policy of linkage tied arms control and trade to Soviet behaviour in other regions. In other words, the US would offer the Soviet Union agreements it wanted only if Moscow behaved well elsewhere.
Nixon visited China from 21 to 28 February 1972 and met Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai. The Shanghai Communiqué set out a process to normalise relations, which also put pressure on the Soviet Union.
Formal US recognition of the People's Republic of China came on 1 January 1979 under Carter, building on Nixon's opening.

Nixon was in Moscow from 22 to 30 May 1972, meeting Leonid Brezhnev, the Soviet leader. The first major arms control agreements, SALT I, were signed there on 26 May 1972, and trade agreements were discussed.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on détente, define it (easing of tension by negotiation, based on balance of power, not trust) and give the dates and places of the key events.

notes.b: The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT) aimed to limit the superpowers' nuclear arsenals. SALT I was the first agreement and it slowed the arms race without ending it.
points: SALT I was signed in Moscow on 26 May 1972 by Nixon and Brezhnev, with Kissinger as the key American negotiator. It had two parts: the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) Treaty and an Interim Agreement.

The ABM Treaty limited missile defence systems. Because each side stayed open to attack, neither could hope to launch a first strike and be safe from retaliation, so deterrence was preserved. The Senate approved it by 88 votes to 2 in August 1972.
The Interim Agreement froze the numbers of land-based ICBMs (intercontinental ballistic missiles) and submarine-launched missile launchers for five years.
It did not limit the number of warheads each missile carried, so MIRVs (multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles) let each side add warheads without breaking the limits.
Both sides therefore kept building up their arsenals, so SALT I limited growth without reducing the number of warheads.
notes.tip: Explaining that SALT slowed growth but did not cut warheads is a concrete mark-earner. Learn the place and date, and name both the ABM Treaty and the Interim Agreement.

notes.b: Détente brought real agreements, but it also drew attacks from critics and was strained by events in the Middle East and Africa.
points: The Helsinki Final Act was signed on 1 August 1975 by 35 states, including the United States and the Soviet Union. It recognised European borders as they stood and set out human rights principles, which the Soviet Union later failed to honour.
Ford and Brezhnev agreed a framework for a second SALT agreement at Vladivostok in November 1974, which kept arms control going after Nixon's fall.

In October 1973 the Yom Kippur War in the Middle East led Nixon to put US forces on alert (DEFCON 3) after Soviet threats of intervention, showing that détente did not remove the risk of confrontation.
The Jackson-Vanik Amendment of 1974 linked US-Soviet trade to freedom of emigration, notably for Soviet Jews. It angered Moscow.

Critics of détente, including conservative Democrats such as Senator Henry Jackson and others on the right, argued that the Soviet Union was gaining military strength while the United States made concessions.
Soviet and Cuban backing for the MPLA in Angola in 1975 and 1976 convinced critics that the Soviet Union was exploiting détente to gain influence in the developing world while talking of peace.
notes.tip: On why détente collapsed, name Afghanistan, Angola and Iran, and the critics' claim of a Soviet build-up. Do not confuse Helsinki (1975, 35 states) with Geneva (1985) or Reykjavik (1986).

notes.h: Carter: human rights, China and Iran, 1977 to 1981
notes.b: Carter came to office stressing moral principles in foreign policy, but events in Iran and Afghanistan pushed him into a harder line.
points: Carter stressed human rights from 1977. He criticised Soviet treatment of dissidents (people who openly oppose their government) such as the physicist Andrei Sakharov, which annoyed Moscow.
He gave full diplomatic recognition to the People's Republic of China on 1 January 1979, building on Nixon's opening.
The Shah of Iran, a US ally who had been deposed, was admitted to the United States in October 1979. In response the US embassy in Tehran was seized on 4 November 1979.
The hostages were held for 444 days and were released on 20 January 1981, the day Reagan took office.

Operation Eagle Claw, a rescue attempt in April 1980, failed: helicopters broke down, and at a desert staging site a helicopter collided with a transport aircraft, killing eight US servicemen. The failure contributed to Carter's defeat in the 1980 election.
notes.tip: Iran is one of the reasons examiners give for the loss of US confidence before Reagan. Use dates: embassy seizure 4 November 1979, rescue attempt April 1980, release 20 January 1981.

notes.h: SALT II, Afghanistan and the end of détente, 1979 to 1980
notes.b: SALT II was meant to build on SALT I, but within months of its signing the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan ended détente.
points: SALT II was signed in Vienna on 18 June 1979 by Carter and Brezhnev. It set an equal ceiling of 2,400 strategic delivery vehicles for each side, to fall to 2,250, and limited multiple-warhead missiles.
Critics, led by Senator Henry Jackson and the Committee on the Present Danger, said SALT II let the Soviet Union keep a lead in heavy land-based missiles, so ratification was in doubt.
Soviet forces entered Afghanistan on 24 and 25 December 1979. Carter condemned the invasion as an unacceptable threat to regional stability, and it ended the era of détente.
SALT II was never ratified. In January 1980 Carter asked the Senate to postpone consideration, because ratification was now politically impossible after Afghanistan.
Carter announced a grain embargo against the Soviet Union in January 1980, which cut off supplies the Soviet Union wanted from the US.
In his State of the Union address in January 1980 he set out the Carter Doctrine: the United States would resist any outside attempt to control the Persian Gulf region.

Carter led a boycott of the Moscow Olympics: the US Olympic Committee voted in April 1980 not to send a team, and dozens of other countries also stayed away. Some national teams, including Britain's, attended despite government pressure.
The Soviet Union and the United States both said they would observe SALT II's limits informally after 1980, but Reagan's government ceased to observe the limits in 1986.
notes.tip: SALT I was 1972, Moscow, Nixon; SALT II was 1979, Vienna, Carter, never ratified. For an Ordinary Level paragraph, say SALT II was never ratified because of Afghanistan.

notes.h: Reagan's rejection of détente and the arms build-up, 1981 to 1985
notes.b: Reagan rejected the logic of détente and deterrence, arguing that the United States should deal with Moscow from strength. This opened what is often called a new Cold War.
points: Reagan described the Soviet Union as an evil empire in his "evil empire" speech, given to the National Association of Evangelicals on 8 March 1983, a phrase that showed how far he had moved from Nixon's approach.
Defence spending rose sharply from 1981 to 1985. Programmes included the B-1 bomber, the MX missile and Pershing II missiles in Western Europe.
American Pershing II and cruise missiles began arriving in Western Europe from late 1983, which led to protests, including at Greenham Common in Britain.
notes.tip: Examiners link Reagan's build-up to the judgement question on why the Cold War ended, so be ready to say what the build-up did to the Soviet Union.

notes.b: Reagan wanted a defence against nuclear missiles instead of relying on the threat of retaliation. His proposal was a big step in technological development, and it also changed the arms talks that followed.
points: Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) in a television address on 23 March 1983, proposing space-based and other systems to destroy incoming missiles.
Critics gave it the nickname Star Wars, after the film, partly because many scientists doubted it could work and partly because of its cost.
It was never deployed, but it alarmed Soviet leaders, who feared an American technological lead they could not match.
SDI also differed from the ABM Treaty of 1972, which had limited defences, and critics said SDI undermined that treaty.
notes.tip: For SDI give the date and medium of the announcement, what it proposed, the nickname, the critics' doubts and that it was never deployed. For Higher Level, add Soviet fears and its role at Reykjavik.

notes.b: A new generation of Soviet leadership made talks possible, and Reagan and Gorbachev then agreed the first treaty to abolish a whole class of nuclear weapons.
points: Brezhnev died in November 1982, and the leadership changed rapidly: Yuri Andropov (to February 1984), Konstantin Chernenko (to March 1985), then Mikhail Gorbachev, who became General Secretary in March 1985.
Gorbachev's policies of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring of the economy) loosened Soviet control over Eastern Europe.
Reagan and Gorbachev met at Geneva in November 1985 and at Reykjavik in October 1986. At Reykjavik they came close to agreeing deep cuts in nuclear weapons.
The Reykjavik talks broke down over SDI: Gorbachev wanted it confined to the laboratory and Reagan refused.

The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty was signed in Washington on 8 December 1987. It eliminated all US and Soviet land-based missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres, with on-site inspection.
It was the first treaty to abolish a whole class of nuclear weapons, unlike SALT, which only limited growth. The Senate ratified it in May 1988.
Reagan spoke at the Berlin Wall (the Brandenburg Gate) on 12 June 1987 and said: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall."
notes.tip: Examiners ask why Reykjavik failed (SDI) and what the INF Treaty did. Say that SALT limited growth, whereas INF eliminated missiles.

notes.h: 1989 and the end of the Cold War
notes.b: In 1989 the division of Europe that defined the Cold War broke up, largely because the Soviet Union stopped using force to hold it together.
points: Soviet troops finished leaving Afghanistan in February 1989, ending the costly war that had begun in December 1979.
The Soviet Union did not intervene when communist governments in Eastern Europe fell during 1989, which was a break with earlier practice, so the changes could go ahead.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, and the collapse of communist governments across Eastern Europe ended the division of the continent.
Reagan's successor, George H. W. Bush, met Gorbachev off Malta on 2 and 3 December 1989, and the two leaders described a new era in relations.
notes.tip: Strong answers name specific events such as INF, Reykjavik and 1989. Do not present Malta as a formal declaration, since it was not a signed statement.

notes.h: Assessment: did the Cold War end because of US policy?
notes.b: Examiners reward judgements that weigh US policy against Soviet internal failure and the choices of Gorbachev, and that also weigh the successes and failures of détente.
points: Achievements of détente and arms control: SALT I, Helsinki, the opening to China and later the INF Treaty. Limits: arsenals kept growing, SALT II was never ratified, and détente had collapsed by 1979.

Supporters of Reagan argue that his build-up and the Strategic Defense Initiative forced the Soviet Union into an arms race it could not afford, and that negotiating from strength created the conditions for Gorbachev's reforms.
Critics of Reagan argue that the Soviet economy was already stagnating before 1980 and that Gorbachev's own reforms were the decisive cause of the change.
Reagan's turn to negotiation owed much to Gorbachev, so critics say the talks were not simply a reward for American strength.
Continuity: détente and arms control created the framework and the habit of verification used in 1987, so the INF Treaty built on the 1970s.
The costs of the Afghan war and falling oil revenues in the mid-1980s added to the Soviet Union's economic difficulties.
Vietnam reduced US willingness to intervene abroad, which affected internationalism. Yet US power and ideas outlasted the Soviet system.
notes.tip: Strong answers weigh Soviet economic collapse against US pressure, and name specific events (INF, Reykjavik, 1989). A sound answer names the leader, the event, the date and one consequence.

keyTerms.definition: The easing of Cold War tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union in the early 1970s through negotiation and arms control.
The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks between the superpowers, which produced SALT I in 1972 and SALT II in 1979, the latter never ratified.
Reagan's 1983 proposal for a space-based missile defence system, nicknamed Star Wars, which was never fully built.
The December 1987 agreement by which the United States and the Soviet Union eliminated their land-based intermediate-range nuclear missiles.
The 1973 law, passed over Nixon's veto, requiring the President to consult Congress and withdraw forces within sixty days unless Congress approved their use.
The advances in weapons and space systems, such as the proposed missile defence and the satellites used for verification, that shaped the arms race of the period.
The continuing US commitment to active engagement in world affairs, which was debated in the 1970s and 1980s as the Vietnam experience made Americans wary of overseas wars.
Kissinger's policy of tying progress on arms control and trade to Soviet behaviour in other regions, such as the Middle East and Africa.

factCards.definition: Carter led a US boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics in protest at the invasion of Afghanistan.

factCards.definition: Reagan used the phrase to describe the Soviet Union on 8 March 1983 in an address to the National Association of Evangelicals.

factCards.definition: Signed on 8 December 1987, it eliminated land-based missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres.
On 12 June 1987 he called on Gorbachev to tear down the Berlin Wall.
In January 1980 Carter declared that the United States would resist any attempt by an outside power to control the Persian Gulf, in response to the Afghan invasion.
Talks broke down in October 1986 because Gorbachev wanted SDI confined to the laboratory and Reagan would not agree.
